topic.subject: science
topic.title: Lightning and earthquakes
topic.scope: static charges, charging by rubbing, lightning and safety, earthquakes, plates, seismograph

nodes.name: Crust is made of tectonic plates

misconceptions.statement: Rubbing creates new charges inside an object that were not there before.
misconceptions.why: Students often think friction 'generates' electricity like a factory rather than moving existing particles.
misconceptions.fix: Rubbing only transfers existing electrons from one object to another; no new charge is created.

probe.question: If you rub a glass rod with silk, where does the positive charge on the rod come from?
probe.wrong_answer: The friction creates the positive charge inside the rod.

misconceptions.root_belief: matter can be created through physical action

misconceptions.statement: Charged objects only attract other things; they do not repel.
misconceptions.why: In everyday life, students see static 'cling' (attraction) more often than active repulsion.
misconceptions.fix: Objects with the same type of charge will push away or repel each other.

probe.question: What happens if two balloons are both rubbed with the same woolen cloth and brought near each other?
probe.wrong_answer: They will stick together because they are both charged.

misconceptions.root_belief: electricity is a force of attraction only

misconceptions.statement: Lightning is a form of fire or burning gas in the sky.
misconceptions.why: Lightning is bright and hot, leading to a visual association with fire.
misconceptions.fix: Lightning is a massive flow of electric charge (discharge) between clouds or cloud and ground.

probe.question: What is lightning made of?
probe.wrong_answer: It is a streak of fire caused by clouds catching flame.

misconceptions.root_belief: bright hot things must be fire

misconceptions.statement: A lightning conductor attracts lightning to the building to stop it from hitting other places.
misconceptions.why: The word 'conductor' and its position on top of buildings suggest it acts like a magnet for lightning.
misconceptions.fix: A lightning conductor provides a safe, low-resistance path for the charge to flow into the ground, protecting the structure.

probe.question: Does a lightning rod increase the chance of your house being hit?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it pulls lightning toward the house.

misconceptions.root_belief: safety devices work by attracting the danger

misconceptions.statement: The Earth's tectonic plates float on a continuous ocean of liquid lava.
misconceptions.why: Diagrams in textbooks often show a bright red mantle, which students interpret as liquid water-like magma.
misconceptions.fix: The mantle is mostly solid rock that can flow very slowly over millions of years; it is not a liquid ocean.

probe.question: What is directly underneath the tectonic plates?
probe.wrong_answer: A sea of liquid melted fire or lava.

misconceptions.root_belief: solid things must float on liquid to move
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

misconceptions.statement: Earthquakes only happen in hot weather or during specific weather changes.
misconceptions.why: Historical myths and the term 'earthquake weather' persist in many cultures, including India.
misconceptions.fix: Earthquakes are caused by internal plate movements and are completely independent of atmospheric weather.

probe.question: Can a heavy rainstorm or a heatwave cause an earthquake?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, earthquakes usually happen when the air is very still and hot.

misconceptions.root_belief: all natural disasters are linked to weather

misconceptions.statement: An earthquake of magnitude 7 is only slightly stronger than one of magnitude 6.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the Richter scale is linear, like a ruler or a marksheet.
misconceptions.fix: The Richter scale is logarithmic; an increase of 2 in magnitude means 1000 times more destructive energy.

probe.question: How much more powerful is a magnitude 8 earthquake compared to a magnitude 6?
probe.wrong_answer: It is about 2 units or 20% stronger.

misconceptions.statement: A charged object cannot attract a neutral (uncharged) object.
misconceptions.why: Students believe that for an electrical force to exist, both objects must already have their own charge.
misconceptions.fix: A charged object can attract an uncharged object by inducing a temporary separation of charges in it.

probe.question: Why does a charged comb pick up tiny bits of uncharged paper?
probe.wrong_answer: The paper must have been secretly charged before the comb touched it.

misconceptions.root_belief: interactions require both parties to have the same property

misconceptions.statement: Tectonic plates are the same thing as the continents.
misconceptions.why: Maps often show plates and continents together, and students only see the land above water.
misconceptions.fix: Tectonic plates are huge slabs of the crust that carry both continents and the ocean floor.

probe.question: Do tectonic plates exist under the Atlantic Ocean?
probe.wrong_answer: No, plates are just the land masses like Asia and Africa.

misconceptions.root_belief: only visible parts of a system exist

misconceptions.statement: Seismographs are used to predict exactly when an earthquake will happen in the future.
misconceptions.why: Confusion between 'recording' an event and 'predicting' an event, similar to weather forecasts.
misconceptions.fix: Seismographs only record the waves of an earthquake that is already happening; we cannot yet predict earthquakes.

probe.question: What is the main purpose of a seismograph?
probe.wrong_answer: To give a warning several days before an earthquake starts.

misconceptions.statement: Wearing rubber shoes makes you completely safe from lightning strikes outdoors.
misconceptions.why: Overgeneralisation of the fact that rubber is an insulator for small household voltages.
misconceptions.fix: Lightning has millions of volts; a thin layer of rubber on shoes cannot stop such a massive discharge.

probe.question: If you are in an open field during a storm, are you safe if you wear sneakers with rubber soles?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because rubber is an insulator and will block the lightning.

misconceptions.root_belief: properties at small scale apply at infinite scale

misconceptions.statement: Static electricity is a 'different' kind of electricity than the one in our wires.
misconceptions.why: The different names ('static' vs 'current') and different sources (rubbing vs batteries) suggest two different substances.
misconceptions.fix: All electricity involves the same electric charges; 'static' just means the charges are not flowing in a continuous circuit.

probe.question: Is the charge on a rubbed balloon the same as the charge moving through a bulb's wire?
probe.wrong_answer: No, static electricity is a different natural force.
